articles.text: In 1960, six-year-old Ruby Bridges became the first Black student to integrate an all-white elementary school in the South. Escorted by U.S. Marshals through angry crowds, Ruby became a national symbol of bravery and hope during the Civil Rights Movement. Her courage has inspired generations to stand up for equality and access to education for all. This Friday, November 14, students, families, and community members are invited to join the Ruby Bridges Walk, led by the Affinity Mentorship Program at Piedmont High School. Participants are encouraged to arrive at 8:00 a.m. in front of Piedmont High School. Affinity Mentorship speakers will begin at 8:05 a.m. before the walk starts. The event celebrates courage, inclusion, and the power of young people to make a difference in their community. The Ruby Bridges Walk honors Ruby’s legacy by inviting students across the country to walk in her name, promoting kindness, inclusion, and the continued fight for justice in education. At Piedmont High, the Affinity Mentorship Program aims to strengthen community connection and emphasize the value of mentorship, representation, and shared action. The program’s student mentors will speak about Ruby’s impact and how her story continues to inspire young leaders today. In May 2018, fifth graders from Martin Elementary School in South San Francisco learned about Ruby and asked their school board to pass a resolution making November 14 Ruby Bridges Day. The annual tradition has expanded since then and Piedmont’s participation began in 2023. All are encouraged to join the Affinity Mentorship team this Friday to honor Ruby Bridges’ courage and walk together toward a more inclusive, compassionate future, one step at a time. articles.text: Editor: This week, PUSD’s School Board will vote on a plan to bring 60 minutes of Latin instruction to the 5th grade schedule next year. As the parent of a current 4th grader, I’ll admit I was surprised when I first heard about this plan. Is a “dead language” really something today’s 11-year-olds need to spend time learning? But after learning more about the district’s rationale for bringing Latin to the 5th grade curriculum, I am impressed and grateful that our district is making this change. Up until this school year, the earliest that PUSD students could start learning a foreign language was 8th grade – putting us behind our peer districts like Orinda and Albany, who begin foreign language in 7th and sometimes 6th grade, and well past the age when young brains are the most plastic and receptive to foreign language acquisition. I was thrilled when Dr. Hawn and the School Board announced last year that they were exploring ways to bring foreign language instruction to the lower grades – and that they worked so quickly to make that priority a reality. Thanks to their efforts, this year’s 7th graders at PMS are now able to take Spanish, Mandarin, or French as an elective – and next year 6th graders will have the same opportunity. Offering foreign language instruction at the elementary level, however, has proven to be a bit more complicated. While most parents expressed interest in Spanish instruction in 5th grade, offering only Spanish in the elementary schools would have a negative impact on French and Mandarin enrollment in secondary school. And logistically the elementary schools are unable to offer all three world languages. Given those constraints, the School Board started exploring Latin instruction for PUSD’s 5th graders. While Latin will only be offered for 60 minutes per week, the district has made a strong case for the potential benefits including improving vocabulary and fostering literacy skills, academic confidence, and cultural awareness. I also really appreciate that our 5th graders will have the shared experience of confronting an entirely new language as their first classroom exposure to a foreign language – especially a language that serves as the foundation for so many other languages they may study in the future. I am thrilled that my daughter will be one of the first PUSD students to receive Latin instruction next year, and I am grateful that our district has continued to find a way to bring foreign language to our younger students. At a time when much of America’s current leadership wants to isolate us from the international community, how wonderful that our district is working to create the next generation of global citizens. — Laura Maestrelli Parent of Havens 4th grader and PMS 7th grader

articles.text: After years of planning and a month of construction, the Linda Beach Tot Lot will open at 10 a.m. Friday, November 14. Mayor Betsy Andersen along with other city staff will host a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the opening of the Tot Lot. The project cost $400,000, with 75% funded by the City’s Facilities Capital Fund, and the remaining 25% from a donation by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). Members of the foundation will be in attendance for the ceremony and will present their $100,000 donation. Patty Dunlap, president of PBF, said she is excited for the opening of the Tot Lot. “PBF is committed to enhancing public spaces throughout Piedmont, including projects that serve children. Safe and friendly play spaces have never been more crucial, as many children are drawn to screens beginning at an early age. Piedmont parks provide a gentle antidote by encouraging connection and creativity outdoors. And it’s not just the kids who benefit – adults need outdoor play time, too.” Dunlap believes tot lots have a positive impact on the community. “The first word that comes to mind is joy,” said Dunlap. “Most people – children for sure – come to a park full of anticipation and energy, knowing they are in for a good time. There is no greater joy than watching a child fully immersed in imaginative play - coasting down a slide, climbing a tree, or trying to touch the sky from a swing. PBF wants to ensure that our parks help create that priceless joy.” The PBF has an extensive history of donating to the creation of tot lots. “PBF has financially contributed to play areas within every major park in the City of Piedmont, including Dracena, the Main Park, and Hampton Field,” said Dunlap. Depending on the upcoming weather for Friday, the grand opening is set for the Linda Beach Tot Lot. Soon, kids will play until their hearts’ content. articles.text: Come meet Baldwin at Oakland Animal Services. Baldwin is a calm and confident 6-year-old German Shepherd Mix. He currently lives in a foster home with cats and kittens and enjoys watching them play. Baldwin’s foster says he is well-mannered, house and crate trained, knows his basic cues, and takes treats gently. He enjoys car rides, walks calmly on leash and is friendly towards people and other dogs when approached. Baldwin, 65-pounds, is a great match for someone looking for an even-keeled, loyal companion. He likes to lean in for pets when people kneel beside him and is happy to hang out without demanding attention, content to just be by someone’s side. You can see more of him in foster on Instagram @catpeoplefosterdogs and on the Oakland Animal Services website. To meet Baldwin, submit your adoption questionnaire online at the shelter’s website and you will be contacted by his foster to arrange a meet-andgreet. The show is a project by award-winning photographers Nicolò Sertorio and J Michael Tucker. People of Faith is a collection of photographs of Oakland faith leaders and will be on view at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church from November 16 to January 18, 2026. The exhibit explores the stories, transformative potential, and roles in the community of Oakland faith leaders, who stand as both anchors and mirrors of their communities, reflecting the struggles, hopes, and transformations taking place around them. The portraits invite viewers to consider the evolving nature of faith in an urban landscape marked by gentrification, inequality, and cultural flux. ‘People of Faith’ aims to question what it means to be a spiritual leader today. articles.text: When the school board voted to remove Health as a required class, the decision seemed straightforward on paper: give students more flexibility and open up space for electives and academic courses. Combined with new AP and honors options at Piedmont High School, students can now take advanced classes earlier than ever. But for many students and teachers, the change signals a shift in what our school values most. At PHS, Health Science fulfills California’s health education requirement through a one-semester course taken in sophomore year. The class goes beyond textbooks and tests, covering topics often overlooked in traditional academics: mental health, stress management, sexual education, healthy relationships, and substance abuse prevention. Health class is the only time in high school where students are explicitly taught how to care for themselves and make informed, real-world decisions. Some sophomores say the class has already had a lasting impact. “I’ve learned things that will carry on with me for a lifetime,” said Quinn Wagener. “The lessons on opioids and drug awareness were eye-opening. I don’t think I’d understand the full picture of drugs and alcohol if I hadn’t taken this class.” “There are so many risks that come with alcohol. At our age, it’s even more likely for someone to be taken advantage of in an intoxicated state,” said sophomore Noah Baldwin. For Health teacher Lael McAuliffe, who works closely with students when they are most vulnerable, removing the requirement is about far more than just scheduling. “This is a significant loss for our students,” she said. “Health education builds a foundation in mental wellness, relationships, and decision-making, skills that research links to better academic and life outcomes.” McAuliffe also warns of the social consequences. “In small Sophomores Andson Zhou, Olivia Bailey, and Diego Branneria present the effects of tobacco usage to the Health Class. Photos by Lael McAuliffe Sophomores George Saunders, Rafeal Rajan, Dahlia Sar-Garza, and Quinn Wagener work with mannequin models to learn about anatomy in Health Science. schools, this can divide students into tracks: those who take accelerated courses and those who don’t. When you take away Health, you take away shared experiences that build empathy and balance,” she said. According to McAuliffe, Health Science functioned as its own department, with a budget of zero dollars. All the models and supplies the students used were either donated by McAuliffe or borrowed from her nonprofit. Even after the class was moved under the Science Department, no funding was added. A small grant from Piedmont Makers covered dissection materials, but only after Health Science applied for it independently. Nonetheless, not all students see the change as a loss. “I would rather take an in-person class that really impacts my future and is something I enjoy,” said Zoya Schulze. “Although Health is important, an online class should suffice for learning the necessary topics.” Senior Mira Sachs chose to skip Health to take Journalism. “They were the same period, and I had no other option,” she said. Though she stands by her choice, Sachs admits missing out on some lessons. “I’m disappointed I didn’t get to take it, but it was the right decision for me at the time.” Flexibility matters, and students deserve choices, but there is a difference between choice and neglect. Every student should have not only the opportunity but the expectation to learn how to manage stress, make healthy decisions, and understand their well-being. Removing Health may open space for electives, but it also strips away structured time to learn how to live well. Even though Health remains technically available, few students are likely to take it once it becomes optional. Under pressure to build “impressive” schedules filled with AP and honors classes, many see Health as expendable. Students may think they’re gaining an academic edge by skipping it, but the cost is steep. Without structured health education, future students risk entering adulthood unprepared to manage stress, navigate relationships, or make informed decisions about their bodies and minds. In a world dominated by social media, misinformation spreads faster than guidance, and peer pressure can easily lead to risky behaviors. Many students also lack the home environment or parental support to fill these gaps, leaving them vulnerable to mistakes with lasting consequences. Neglecting to invest in students’ well-being creates a gap not only in practical knowledge but in confidence, resilience, and the ability to navigate adulthood: advantages no GPA can measure. class, the school board is failing students, prioritizing academics over essential life skills and leaving them unprepared for the realities of college and beyond. As senior Samantha Huynh said, “Some of the topics taught in Health, like Sex-Ed, might not be relevant to all of us right now, but these life skills will become crucial for every one of us in the future.”

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Advanced Acting class will present four showings of the comedy Noises Off at the Alan Harvey Theatre this weekend. Four-time nominee of best play, Noises Off, written by Michael Frayn, is considered one of the best farces ever written. The shows are set for Thursday, November 13 through Sunday, November 16. Noises Off is a hilarious backstage comedy about a small theater company struggling to put on a play. The chaotic play-within-aplay gives the audience a glimpse of what putting on a show is like, from a shaky tech rehearsal to performances on a tour that completely fall apart. Forgotten lines, misplaced props, slamming doors and messy relationships ultimately lead to total chaos. Prior to leaving for college, recent PHS graduate Noah Bruggeman built the set with longtime construction coach and director, Bob Moorhead. The pair, along with PHS stagecraft students, spent hours crafting the elaborate two-story set for Noises Off, which features numerous stairways, doors and passageways that the cast runs, walks, and falls through during the show. The set is practically a character in the play, as it features seven doors, three staircases, and it turns 180 degrees to allow the audience to see the play onstage as well as backstage. Sparrow Lieu, who plays Poppy Norton-Taylor, the anxious assistant, says “Noises Off is ridiculously funny and complicated. The tangled relationships between characters combined with slapstick comedy shows the audience the true value of resilience.” Sacha Andrews, who plays Brooke Ashton, the ditzy and clueless cast member, says that everyone should come see the show. “It has super cool sets, costumes, and character choices. It’s a really fun show, especially for people who have any interest in theatre.” Noises Off contains humor about sexual innuendos, and is a slapstick comedy that is appropriate for ages 10 and up. For more information or questions. contact director Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us. All shows are at the Alan Harvey Theatre at Piedmont High School, 800 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: Everywhere I turn lately, I hear the same thing: “I just want to feel connected again.” It’s there in conversations with friends, at work, and even in the media. People miss being together. We miss laughing in the same room, sharing real moments, feeling part of something bigger than ourselves. But connection doesn’t just appear out of nowhere. Someone has to start it, and that takes courage. It takes courage to send the text. It takes courage to invite people over (even if you don’t have time to clean your house). It takes courage to be the one who says, “Hey, want to get together?” without knowing who will say yes. Sure, you could wait for someone else to make the first move, but connection only grows when someone chooses to go first. And that person might need to be you. So what does that look like in real life? Here are three simple ways to start: 1. Keep it simple. Connection doesn’t need a theme or a color palette. It just needs an opening. Invite a couple of friends for tea. Meet at the park. Send the message that says, “Want to catch up?” The less complicated it is, the more likely it will actually happen. Simplicity makes connection possible. 2. Don’t let setbacks stop you. Sometimes people won’t respond. Sometimes plans fall through. That’s okay. It’s not a reflection of your worth or your effort. Keep trying. Keep inviting. Keep showing up. Courage isn’t about never feeling awkward—it’s about choosing to keep reaching out even though you know it might feel awkward. 3. Look for novelty. New experiences spark connection. Invite someone to try a pottery class, take a spontaneous day trip somewhere new, or explore a new walking path. Novelty wakes up the brain and gives people something to share, laugh about, and remember. It doesn’t have to be big, just different enough to feel fresh. So if you’ve been waiting for a sign to reach out, this is it. Don’t wait for perfect—just start. That one small act of courage might be exactly what someone else has been waiting for, too. Nina Meehan is a coach, speaker and workshop facilitator with expertise in creativity, connection and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: Piedmont High’s doubles team of Samantha Huynh and Emma Chan made school history at the Western Alameda County Conference on Friday and Saturday, November 7-8 at Chabot College in Hayward. The duo battled their way to win the Foothill Division’s doubles bracket, the first girls’ team in school history to win the doubles title since the league’s inception in 2012. Piedmont has reached the WACC doubles final four times – 2016 (Hannah Marcus/Sophia Landes), 2018 (Kiana Kasrovi/ Audrey Call), 2019 (Call/Marlowe McEffee), and in 2024 with Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum – but never won it. That came to an end on Saturday. “I had no clue that we’re the first. It’s funny because I’m writing the five things I wanted to accomplish for our senior yearbook, and winning the WACC was at the top of my list. It’s just so meaningful for me as a senior to have this. I’m really proud of it,” Huynh said. “Going into the tournament, I didn’t really have any expectations. Going in unseeded, I didn’t want to get my hopes up for something that wasn’t guaranteed to happen. I tried to take things match by match,” Chan added. The pair defeated Alameda’s No. 2 seed Natalie Wong and Sophie Featherstone in the finals, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3. To get there, they defeated Naomi Lin and Caroline Sue of Alameda 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinals, won 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 over No. 4 seed Fiona Wood and Sloane Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in the quarterfinals, and opened the tournament with a heated 4-6, 6-2, 14-12 win over Berkeley’s Esra Abarbanel and Vera Ertel. Despite being Piedmont’s No. 1 doubles team throughout the season, Chan and Huynh entered the bracket as an unranked team. Perhaps the chemistry they established this year was a catalyst to their performance in the tournament, where doubles teams like Alameda’s are filled with the team’s best singles players. “It’s really special. In the finals, we played two singles players. It was obviously very challenging and it demonstrates how it’s a common strategy for the tournament. Sam and I were already in-synch this season, and this tournament showed how connected our play is. Sam knew when to switch sides every single time, I didn’t even have to say anything,” Chan said. “I knew it has been a while since an unseeded team has won. We were a little surprised we were unseeded. Once we beat the No. 4 seed, we really gained a lot of momentum,” Huynh added. The Highlanders received the No. 12 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section Team Championship and hosted No. 5 Northgate on Tuesday, November 11. articles.text: Lagios, Henderson lead Highlanders in offensive outburst Staff Photos Jimmy Lagios completed 10 of 13 passes for 219 yards and four touchdowns against Newark Memorial. Piedmont’s football team ended its regular season on Friday, November 7 with a commanding 42-28 win over Newark Memorial at the Cougars’ home field. The Highlanders go into North Coast Section with a 6-4 overall record. Piedmont received a berth in the Division 7 NCS bracket as the No. 3 seed for the second straight season. They are set to visit No. 7 St. Patrick in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. The Bruins earned home field advantage after winning the Tri-County League title. Piedmont had a slow start against Newark and trailed 14-0 before coming to life. They scored 28 straight points before the Cougars’ next score. It was a big game for quarterback Jimmy Lagios and running back Xavier Henderson. Lagios had just three incomplete passes, recording 219 passing yards and four touchdowns, average 21.9 yards per completion. Henderson, meanwhile, was back in the lineup after missing the last game due to an injury. He recorded 142 yards and two touchdowns on 10 carries. Game Recap Newark Memorial struck first on its first drive of the game with a six-yard touchdown carry. After a turnover on downs at Piedmont’s own 30, the Cougars scored again in four plays to go up 14-0, but the comeback was on from there. PHS scored on a seven-play series, which started with a 45-yard run by Henderson to the Newark 25. Henderson capped off the drive with a one-yard dive after coming in motion to take the snap, making it a 14-7 deficit near the end of the first quarter. On the ensuing drive, Piedmont’s Henry Brennan forced a fumble that was recovered by Rehan Mumtaz at NMHS’ 44 early in the second. PHS scored on just three plays, where Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a 25-yard seam down the middle, making it 14-13 after a blocked extra point. Newark went three-and-out, leading to a 51-yard touchdown pass from Lagios to Cash Panico on their very first play to give Piedmont a 20-14 lead. On the play, Panico made an athletic catch to high-point the football, leading to a catch and run to the end zone. After trading possession to end the first half, PHS started the third quarter with a 55-yard, fourplay touchdown drive. Henderson scored on a 20-yard carry, breaking a tackle and dragging another defender into the end zone, while he converted a two-point run to make it 28-14. Newark got one back in the third quarter on a four-play, 68 yard drive to put itself behind one possession at 29-21. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ team placed second at the WACC Championship. Pictured are Leighton Mand (left), Skylar Best, Amalia Gray, Kelsey Coleman, Cora Chun, Viviane Oesterer, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Piedmont High’s cross-country team returned to Hayward High on Saturday, November 8, for the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference Championships. The girls’ team placed second among six schools, while the boys’ team placed fifth. The girls’ team trailed Berkeley High in scoring by five points. “Only Berkeley beat us, a school with over 3000 students. It showed the strength of the girls’ team, especially in the Division 4 category. I’ve got to say, even though many of the varsity girls did not run distance personal best times, they sure raced hard, especially in the latter part of the race,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s football team ended its regular season on Friday, November 7 with a commanding 42-28 win over Newark Memorial at the Cougars’ home field. The Highlanders go into North Coast Section with a 6-4 overall record. Piedmont received a berth in the Division 7 NCS bracket as the No. 3 seed for the second straight season. They are set to visit No. 7 St. Patrick in Vallejo on Friday, November 14. The Bruins earned home field advantage after winning the Tri-County League title. Piedmont had a slow start against Newark and trailed 14-0 before coming to life. They scored 28 straight points before the Cougars’ next score. It was a big game for quarterback Jimmy Lagios and running back Xavier Henderson. Lagios had just three incomplete passes, recording 219 passing yards and four touchdowns, average 21.9 yards per completion. Henderson, meanwhile, was back in the lineup after missing the last game due to an injury. He recorded 142 yards and two touchdowns on 10 carries. After a turnover on downs at Piedmont’s own 30, the Cougars scored again in four plays to go up 14-0, but the comeback was on from there. PHS scored on a seven-play series, which started with a 45-yard run by Henderson to the Newark 25. articles.text: Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, was recently named to the Pacific International League’s All-League team. RBIs, one triple, and four home Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, is currently a junior at Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, where he is the baseball team’s third baseman. Over the summer, Aikawa kept his skills sharp with the DubSea Fish Sticks of the Pacific International League, a premier summer collegiate baseball league in the Northwest. The Pacific International League recently named Aikawa to its All-League Team for his performance last summer. The Fish Sticks captured the PIL Championship on August 2 with a dominant 18–1 win over the Gumberoos; their first title since the team’s founding in 2015. The 33-year-old Pacific International League typically attracts college players from across the Pacific Northwest. It is a semi-professional league, with most participants unpaid to preserve NCAA eligibility. The league also offers a unique mix, with former Major League players competing alongside recent college graduates. As a sophomore at Lewis & Clark, Aikawa earned All-Northwest Conference honors last season. The Pioneers finished 20–19, with Aikawa leading the team in several categories. Aikawa led the Pioneers with a .372 batting average, 54 hits, and 14 doubles. He also recorded 35 runs, 37 runs. He was the Piedmont Post’s 2021 Sophomore of the Year and an influential four-year starter for the Highlanders. He earned second-team All-League honors as a senior and was first-team in 2022. Aikawa contributed both as a shortstop and pitcher in 2023, closing the year as Piedmont’s leading hitter with a .357 average, 25 hits, 12 doubles, one home run, 13 RBIs, and 22 runs scored. As a pitcher, he led the way with 37 innings, a 4–2 record, 44 strikeouts, and a 1.324 ERA, even though it was his first year on the mound for the Highlanders. After a successful drive collecting gear earlier this fall, the youth-led nonprofit set up a booth at the Oakland Roots Family Appreciation Night at the Oakland Coliseum on October 25, collecting more gently used soccer gear and spreading awareness about their cause. This season, Next Gen Soccer is expanding its efforts to include pinnies from recreation clubs throughout the East Bay that have only seen one or two seasons of use. By recirculating these items, the group hopes to ease the financial burden on families and reduce textile waste, keeping still-useful gear in play rather than in storage or landfills. articles.text: Vienna Boys Choir The world-renowned Vienna Boys Choir returns to UC Berkeley for a special performance celebrating the 200th birthday of composer Johann Strauss Jr. The concert, titled “Strauss For Ever,” takes place this Sunday, November 16 at 3 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall. Presented by Cal Performances as part of its “Vocal Celebration / Family” series, the event showcases Strauss Jr.’s timeless compositions through the pure, soaring voices of one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious boys’ choirs. The program includes familiar favorites such as The Blue Danube, Tales from the Vienna Woods, and a lively mix of polkas. Founded in 1498, the Vienna Boys Choir has performed across the globe, preserving Austria’s rich musical heritage. The group, made up of boys aged 9 to 14 from various countries, is known for its crystal-clear tone, precision, and spirited performances. The choir has been singing choral arrangements of Strauss’s music since the 1920s. “Strauss For Ever” offers audiences a unique opportunity to hear the signature waltz and polka sounds of Vienna reimagined through youthful voices, serving as an homage to a composer who helped define his city’s cultural identity. Tickets are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday through Friday, 12 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.

articles.text: Museo Italo Americano, the first museum in the United States devoted exclusively to Italian and Italian-American art and culture, is hosting a holiday artisan market at San Francisco’s historic Fort Mason Saturday, December 6 and Sunday, December 7. The Mercatino di Natale, or Italian Christmas Market, welcomes local vendors and artists selling Italian food, fashion, jewelry, art and one-of-a-kind crafts. Proceeds from the Mercatino benefit the Museo’s historical and cultural programs as well as participating Italian and Italian-American artists, and serves as a unique holiday shopping experience. The two-day event is held in the museum from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. on December 6, and 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on December 7. Museo Italo Americano was founded in 1978 above a café in the city’s North Beach neighborhood, San Francisco’s Italian-American enclave. The museum’s mission is to research, collect and display works by Italian and Italian-American artists, and to promote language courses, lectures and educational programs. Through its permanent collection, historical archive and community programs like Mercatino, the museum aims to preserve and share the rich heritage of Italian-Americans for Bay Area residents. For more information, visit https://museoitaloamericano.org.

articles.text: Kate Winslet and Idris Elba in The Mountain Between Us The Mountain Between Us is an apt title that neatly captures the film’s essence—from its opening setup to the final frame. It follows a familiar survival-and-romance template, but remains solidly entertaining thanks to two superb performances. Dr. Ben Bass (Idris Elba) and Alex Martin (Kate Winslet) meet by chance at the Boise, Idaho airport after their respective flights are canceled. Ben, a neurosurgeon, must reach Baltimore via Denver to perform a lifesaving operation, while Alex, a photojournalist, is trying to get to her own wedding. They decide to charter a private plane piloted by an old-timer (Beau Bridges) who brings along his golden Labrador. Everything goes according to plan—until it doesn’t. When their small aircraft crashes on a snow-covered mountain range in the dead of winter, survival becomes the only priority. The story unfolds on two levels. The first is a gripping tale of endurance reminiscent of The Revenant: the cold is punishing, the terrain treacherous, and their chances slim. With Alex’s leg badly injured, Ben must decide whether to stay with the wreckage and hope for rescue or attempt a desperate trek through the wilderness. The second thread, equally compelling, explores the growing bond between Alex and Ben. Amid exhaustion, injury and isolation, attraction simmers beneath their shared determination to survive. articles.text: The Disney animated feature James and the Giant Peach is based on Roald Dahl’s beloved 1961 children’s book. Like most well-crafted films made for young audiences, it casts a spell—even when it turns a bit scary. But then, kids like a touch of fright if it’s wrapped in fairy-tale fantasy. The story, both outlandish and humorous, centers on a British orphan, James (Paul Terry), who has lost his once-doting parents and now lives on a mountaintop with two sadistic aunts, Spiker and Sponge (Joanna Lumley and Miriam Margolyes). They’ve turned the boy into a chore servant, callously ignoring his grief and loneliness. One day, a strange old man (Pete Postlethwaite) gives James a bag of magical crocodile tongues, which he accidentally spills on the ground. The mixture fertilizes a barren peach tree, producing a single enormous fruit. Inside the giant peach, James finds sanctuary—and a family of human-sized insects, including a brash centipede, an aristocratic caterpillar, a sultry spider, a matronly ladybug, a wise green grasshopper, a glowworm, and an earthworm. When the aunts come looking for James, the centipede cuts the peach’s stem in panic, sending it rolling down the hill and into the ocean. There, the peach transforms into a floating airship, carrying James and his insect companions across the sea toward New York City. What follows is a classic children’s adventure filled with chases, escapes, a mechanical shark, ghostly pirates, and magical flights—all leading to a climactic arrival at the Empire State Building and a daring rescue by the fire department. As in any good fairy tale, the ending is sweetly satisfying. James, surrounded by his new family of friends, settles into a cozy cottage in Central Park— finally home. James and the Giant Peach. pages.text: Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesdays: a dry stroll through Piedmont’s past By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group thought their luck had run out last week. Forecasts called for heavy rain just as they were set to start their walk, and yet, as they like to say, it never rains on Wednesday mornings in Piedmont. True to form, the skies stayed dry. Twenty-seven walkers and two loyal K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra under gray clouds and a brisk breeze. The group welcomed a special visitor, Aliza Kazmi, Director of Community Partnerships for Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas. Kazmi had heard about Walking on Wednesdays and came to experience it firsthand. After introductions, she shared updates on the supervisor’s work around housing, food insecurity, and immigration — and joined the walk herself. Originally, the group had planned to check on the City’s first bioswale at Fairview and Grand, which they’d last visited during a storm. But with no rain in sight, plans shifted. A story in that morning’s Piedmont Post mentioned a new plaque marking the 2024 planting of an Island Oak at the Mountain/Bellevue Circle. The oak replaced the city’s original Holiday Tree, a giant sequoia that once lit Piedmont winters until World War II blackout precautions ended the tradition. Removed in 2023 after it began to topple, the tree had stood for nearly a century. Curious to see the new plaque, the walkers headed up Mountain Avenue. Along the way, they admired a life-size statue of a greenish gentleman clad in leaves and noted an unusual telephone Wednesday, November 12, 2025 21 Features pole fashioned from a dead tree trunk. But when they reached the circle, the plaque was nowhere to be found. Later, City Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent confirmed it was simply hidden under a traffic cone — safe, if not yet on display. With time and dry skies to spare, the group continued along Sea View Avenue, where the story of early Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander came up. His estate, “Brown Gables,” once stretched from what’s now 87 Sea View to Hampton Avenue. After Alexander’s death in 1939, his widow honored his wish to tear down the mansion so the land could be divided into family lots. That’s why homes in the middle of the block look newer than the grand old houses nearby. The walkers followed Hampton Road to Crocker Park, home to Benny Bufano’s Bear and Nursing Cubs sculpture. The Italian-born Modernist’s two-and-a-half-ton granite bear, one of 25, has stood there since 1980, joining works by Bufano now held in major museums across the country. The group finished their walk with a stop at the home of sculptor Jeremy Bo Droga and his wife, Marie-Elise. Their historic Albert Farr–designed home was completed just before the 1906 earthquake. In 2023, the Drogas gave the walkers a tour of their newly completed garage — a soaring, light-filled space with room for six cars, a spiral staircase to a rooftop garden, and drought-tolerant landscaping. Returning to the city center via Wildwood, Sheridan, and Highland avenues, the walkers reflected on how a day that began with storm warnings turned into a dry, improvisational tour of art, architecture, and history — the kind of walk that makes Wednesdays in Piedmont feel special. Walking on Wednesdays meets at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra, corner of Highland and Magnolia. Everyone, including friendly dogs, is welcome. articles.text: There was a large turnout of 26 readers on the patio of the Piedmont Community Hall on November 3 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s monthly First Mondays Reading Group. Usual discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus was away, so Lois Price filled in. The group met to discuss their November book, Euphoria by Lily King. Lois began with background on the novel, published in 2015, which tells the story of three young anthropologists in the 1930s caught in a love triangle. It is a story of desire, possession and discovery, inspired by events in the life of anthropologist Margaret Mead. In the novel, English anthropologist Andrew Bankson has spent years in isolation studying a tribe along New Guinea’s Sepik River with little success. Lonely and near despair, he meets the famous Nell Stone and her husband Fen. Bankson is drawn to the couple—especially Nell— and his life gains new purpose. The pair, meanwhile, are hungry for discovery, and Bankson leads them to a female-dominated tribe. Their groundbreaking research will make history but not without sacrifice and harm. Some readers were captivated while others felt left out. A few found the story confusing at first because Euphoria isn’t historical fiction. King drew inspiration from Margaret Mead and her circle, creating a three-part story about anthropology, culture and relationships. Some who didn’t like the book found it tedious and juvenile, with little action until Chapter 27. They couldn’t relate to the characters and found it difficult to connect with the story. Some felt King’s character development was lacking, while others thought it well done. Readers also discussed the moral implications of researchers inserting themselves into Indigenous societies and the impact on those cultures. The group wondered whether it is ever possible to truly understand another culture—or even other people. Those who enjoyed Euphoria found it compelling and felt the tension between the characters carried the story. For them, the action at the book’s end was less important than the emotional undercurrents. They praised King’s use of alternating voices—Bankson’s male narrative and Nell’s journal entries— to move the story forward. While not a Mead biography, the book offered a dreamy snapshot of her era. Some wished the connection to Mead were more explicit rather than imagined. The discussion turned to the motivations of anthropologists. Are they driven by curiosity, fame or self-understanding? Readers also questioned why King implied a link to Mead— was it to add intrigue or sell more books? As the discussion progressed, it became clear that readers’ personal experiences shaped their responses to Euphoria. Those who had followed Margaret Mead, studied anthropology or traveled to Papua New Guinea found it especially engaging. One such reader, Orrel Lanter, visited the islands in the late 1970s while sourcing beans for her coffee business. articles.text: Part 3: Ascent of 18,150-foot mountain in May 2017 Outside the village of Terskol spectacular views were plentiful. Piedmont’s Bill Baringer continued his high-altitude world tour with a climb to the European zenith, Mt. Elbrus in Russia. At an elevation of 18,510 feet it is the highest peak on the European continent. His ascent came just three months after scaling South America’s tallest peak, Mt. Aconcagua in Argentina, a 22,840-foot beast. For this trip, Baringer elected to take his skis. His 11-day journey began in the village of Terskol, at the ski lodge Nakra, where Baringer and his new colleagues spent four nights to acclimate. Each day, Bill and company would embark on elevation acclimatization hikes. Their sleeping lodge was at 6,700 feet, but within four days their bodies needed to be ready for the thin air at their next base camp at 12,600 feet. After three days, their guide, Sasha, developed a cold and informed the team that the assistant guide, Sasha 2, would be taking over. With only one guide now, Sasha 2, Baringer and his climbing party decided to hire another assistant guide for the summit day. the next hut more than two miles above sea level. The huts were steel shipping containers which made for a luxurious stay, especially when compared to the tents on his climb in Argentina. But the group found it difficult to sleep after arriving at the new 12,600- foot altitude. Baringer recalled being surprised at how relaxed the guides were when he asked if he could go off alone for a ski expedition. “Sasha 2 didn’t look outside to check the weather or visibility (which hadn’t improved); he didn’t ask if I’d be able to navigate back to the hut on my own and avoid the steep, crevassed slopes on either side of the intended route. He just reminded me that dinner would be at 7 p.m.,” Baringer said. Bill Baringer juggles snowballs during some downtime on the climb of Mt. Elbrus. The trail to the top of Mt. Elbrus went past amazing rock formations caused by a particular cooling sequence of molten lava from the mountain’s volcanic origin. Elbrus, near the Georgian border between the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, is prone to whiteouts and avalanches, and is wrinkled with dangerous crevasses. More mountaineers die on Elbrus every year than on Everest. But in Russia they let Baringer go solo, without a map or communication device. Baringer applied skins to the bottom of his telemark skis, set his Garmin GPS and headed into Russian’s upper reaches all alone. “When I first met Bill, I thought this guy was nuts for wanting to ski down this mountain, but I soon realized just how much preparation he had done for this,” said hiker Donovan Kowloon. Baringer made it back fine, despite the low visibility and losing the path at times. The Russian hiking company’s itinerary to reach the summit was unconventional, but provided some comfort. They hiked up a portion of the mountain for the day, then trekked back down to rest overnight. The next day they loaded themselves, food, fuel, cookware, and equipment into the ski resort’s gondola, and then into a snowcat to get dropped off at the previous day’s altitude. After two days, Baringer made it to the higher Muzafar huts, also shipping containers, at 13,450 feet. The second to last ascent day the group made it to 15,300 feet, then went back down to rest. Baringer and his hiking companions rose well before the sun at 2:00 a.m. for a 3:00 a.m. snowcat ride to their previous elevation. Their summit day started off with an unplanned 40-minute wait for the snowcat to arrive. The weather was clear, but reports of an incoming snowstorm made the delay anxiety inducing. Wearing headlamps, they finally began their ascent at 4:00 Bill Baringer follows Australian climber Mary Lum near the summit of Mt. Elbrus. a.m. Baringer opted for double boots and crampons, with skis on his back for the descent. A scary moment occurred at an icy portion of the mountain when a hiker in the group in front of them slipped. Unable to stop himself with an ice axe the man tumbled and slid down 150 feet, finally stopping with a large poof of snow. Luckily his fall ended in soft snow and he was okay. But the accident provided a wake-up call for everyone on the mountain. For safety Baringer’s group decided to tie each other together with rope; but when there wasn’t enough rope, Baringer and Kowloon went without. “Bill was very brave. He led our group up almost the whole way, frequently checking back on everyone to make sure we hadn’t gotten too far away from the group,” said fellow climber Kowloon. Nearing the summit, the wind and clouds picked up, making it difficult to see the red wands in the snow delineating the path to the top. Given the icy conditions, Baringer knew skiing back down would not be possible, but the goal and continent number three were in the books. At 10:15 a.m. on May 6, 2017, Bill Baringer crested the peak of Mt. Elbrus at 18,510 feet above sea level. Bill brandished a copy of the Piedmont Post and held up three fingers to mark the conquest of the highest peak on a third continent. NEXT WEEK: Part 4 of Bill Baringer’s campaign to climb the highest peak of each continent. In January 2018 he climbed the 16,050-foot Vinson Massif in Antarctica. Note: Last week’s coverage mistakenly reported Mount Aconcagua, the highest point in South America, was located in Peru. It is located in Argentina, in the Mendoza Province, within the Andes mountain range. Bill Baringer takes a break from hiking for some high-altitude skiing. Bill Baringer stands atop Mt. Elbrus with a copy of the Piedmont Post.

Their sleeping lodge was at 6,700 feet, but within four days their bodies needed to be ready for the thin air at their next base camp at 12,600 feet. After three days, their guide, Sasha, developed a cold and informed the team that the assistant guide, Sasha 2, would be taking over. With only one guide now, Sasha 2, Baringer and his climbing party decided to hire another assistant guide for the summit day. By day five they climbed to the next hut more than two miles above sea level. The huts were steel shipping containers which made for a luxurious stay, especially when compared to the tents on his climb in Argentina. But the group found it difficult to sleep after arriving at the new 12,600- foot altitude. Baringer recalled being surprised at how relaxed the guides were when he asked if he could go off alone for a ski expedition. “Sasha 2 didn’t look outside to check the weather or visibility (which hadn’t improved); he didn’t ask if I’d be able to navigate back to the hut on my own and avoid the steep, crevassed slopes on either side of the intended route. He just reminded me that dinner would be at 7 p.m.,” Baringer said. Bill Baringer juggles snowballs during some downtime on the climb of Mt. Elbrus. The trail to the top of Mt. Elbrus went past amazing rock formations caused by a particular cooling sequence of molten lava from the mountain’s volcanic origin. Elbrus, near the Georgian border between the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, is prone to whiteouts and avalanches, and is wrinkled with dangerous crevasses. More mountaineers die on Elbrus every year than on Everest. But in Russia they let Baringer go solo, without a map or communication device. Baringer applied skins to the bottom of his telemark skis, set his Garmin GPS and headed into Russian’s upper reaches all alone. “When I first met Bill, I thought this guy was nuts for wanting to ski down this mountain, but I soon realized just how much preparation he had done for this,” said hiker Donovan Kowloon. Baringer made it back fine, despite the low visibility and losing the path at times. The Russian hiking company’s itinerary to reach the summit was unconventional, but provided some comfort. They hiked up a portion of the mountain for the day, then trekked back down to rest overnight. The next day they loaded themselves, food, fuel, cookware, and equipment into the ski resort’s gondola, and then into a snowcat to get dropped off at the previous day’s altitude. After two days, Baringer made it to the higher Muzafar huts, also shipping containers, at 13,450 feet. The second to last ascent day the group made it to 15,300 feet, then went back down to rest. Baringer and his hiking companions rose well before the sun at 2:00 a.m. for a 3:00 a.m. snowcat ride to their previous elevation. Their summit day started off with an unplanned 40-minute wait for the snowcat to arrive. The weather was clear, but reports of an incoming snowstorm made the delay anxiety inducing. Wearing headlamps, they finally began their ascent at 4:00 Bill Baringer follows Australian climber Mary Lum near the summit of Mt. Elbrus. a.m. Baringer opted for double boots and crampons, with skis on his back for the descent. A scary moment occurred at an icy portion of the mountain when a hiker in the group in front of them slipped. Unable to stop himself with an ice axe the man tumbled and slid down 150 feet, finally stopping with a large poof of snow. Luckily his fall ended in soft snow and he was okay. But the accident provided a wake-up call for everyone on the mountain. For safety Baringer’s group decided to tie each other together with rope; but when there wasn’t enough rope, Baringer and Kowloon went without. “Bill was very brave. He led our group up almost the whole way, frequently checking back on everyone to make sure we hadn’t gotten too far away from the group,” said fellow climber Kowloon. Nearing the summit, the wind and clouds picked up, making it difficult to see the red wands in the snow delineating the path to the top. Given the icy conditions, Baringer knew skiing back down would not be possible, but the goal and continent number three were in the books. At 10:15 a.m. on May 6, 2017, Bill Baringer crested the peak of Mt. Elbrus at 18,510 feet above sea level. Bill brandished a copy of the Piedmont Post and held up three fingers to mark the conquest of the highest peak on a third continent. articles.text: Maria Carson-Breber passed away in her Piedmont home on September 19, 2025 at the age of 61 after a three-year battle with ovarian cancer. Maria Erin Carson was born June 2, 1964 in Maryland to parents Tom and Mary. Soon after, the family moved to San Jose, CA where Maria grew up as the eldest sister to her three brothers and her cousin Judy. Maria attended Queen of Apostles School before graduating from Lynbrook High where she was a three-sport athlete and won a Junior Achievement national award for her business startup. After graduating from UC Davis with a degree in Economics, she worked at Intel and Lucasfilm before moving to the East Coast for graduate school in 1990. Maria found her people and her passion at Harvard’s School of Education. The “Boston Girls” became her lifelong friends and a year of research with breast cancer patients at the Medical School led to her love of bringing clarity to difficult decisions. During the summer of 1995 while working as a management consultant near Boston, she went to a co-worker’s surprise 30th birthday party and met Pierre, up from Houston and boldly wearing a cowboy hat. It was love at first sight and, after a few months traveling to see each other, Maria and Pierre were soon living together in Houston. They became engaged in Paris and were married in San Francisco. A year later, Maria and Pierre moved to Berkeley, CA and started a family with the births of Emma and Carson. In 2003, the family moved to Aberdeen, Scotland and returned two years later with Maria pregnant with Ben and a new home in Piedmont. In 2011, the family was again on the move to Bangkok, Thailand before returning in 2014 and settling in Piedmont. With three young children and multiple moves, Maria’s professional life took a back seat to raising a family. Yet Maria found time for part-time consulting work to companies, Piedmont’s Maria Carson-Breber and husband Pierre Breber. Maria Carson-Breber School District and Planning and Recreation Departments, and individuals through her business. Decide LLC. Maria’s proprietary decision-making process and her unique listening and facilitation skills helped hundreds get unstuck and move forward with a decision. Her greatest satisfaction came from helping many high school seniors decide where to go to college, usually after weeks of anxiety and within days of the deadline. After a few hours with Maria and often through tears, the seniors would emerge with conviction about their future plans and a hug to show their deep appreciation for Maria’s special talent. A lifelong exerciser, Maria made close friends on her Masters swimming teams and in her spin classes, and she became a devoted user of Peloton. But many will remember Maria for her brutal pace on walks along the beach and up and down the hills of Piedmont wearing a big floppy sun hat. Friends remember Maria as thoughtful and insightful, gracious and kind, interesting and interested, warm and empathetic, welcoming and caring, trustworthy and generous, curious and compassionate. She was a bright light who greeted you with a smile, a positive force who made everyone feel special, and someone who could turn strangers into friends. Family remembers Maria as all that and the most loving and supportive wife and mother, daughter and sister, aunt and cousin. She was the best mother to her children: unconditionally patient, caring and encouraging. Maria is survived by her husband Pierre, children Emma, Carson and Ben, parents Tom and Mary, brothers Tom, Chris and Tim, sister/cousin Judy, and many cousins, nieces, and nephews. A Celebration of Life will be held at 3 pm on Tuesday, November 25 at Piedmont Community Church. A reception will follow at the Piedmont Community Hall. Business casual attire suggested (no tie for men). The service will be recorded for outof-towners. Maria would want families to stay together during Thanksgiving week!

articles.text: Colleen Hoffman, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, sister, and friend, passed away peacefully on September 19, 2025, surrounded by her three daughters and filled with the love, faith, and gratitude that shaped her life. She moved through the world with courage, strength, optimism, and grace, qualities that illuminated her path through the challenges and quiet beauty of her later years. Born in Oakland, California, in 1936 to Gertrude and Thomas Pugh, Colleen was the second of six children. She took pride in her role as “big sister,” serving as loyal mentor, confidant, playmate, and friend. As a young girl, she loved dance and drama and created her own small dance school to teach ballet to the neighborhood children. At age 11 years her Bible was inscribed, “To Colleen Pugh, for faithful attendance,” reflecting a devotion to faith that remained steady throughout her life. As a young woman, Colleen worked as a runway model and instructor at the John Robert Powers Modeling and Charm School. Her outer beauty was equally matched by a depth of character, humility, and integrity. She had an extraordinary gift for bringing out the best in others, a quality that continued to shine throughout her life as a mother, wife, friend, and leader. In 1960, Colleen married Mark Hoffman, beginning a 41-year partnership marked by deep love and a shared devotion to family, friends, art, and community. Together they created a warm and loving home that became the hub for lively dinner parties, large holiday gatherings, and endless celebrations where Colleen would deliver heartfelt toasts honoring each guest at the table. She embraced every stage of her children’s lives, encouraging them in their pursuits and taking genuine interest in their friends. She taught Sunday School at St. John’s Episcopal Church, served on the PTA, led Brownie and Girl Scout troops, and assumed the role of enthusiastic cheerleading coach for her daughters and their friends. Her grandchildren and great-grandchildren, 20 in all, adored their “Grandma Colleen” who was known for her delicious Rice Crispy chicken, whimsical pancakes, and cozy sleepovers. They loved their adventures with Grandma that included rides in cabs, buses, trains, planes, boats and cable cars, visiting parks, zoos, Broadway Musicals, and museums. Together, they indulged in Fenton’s ice cream sundaes, screamed with delight on Disneyland roller coaster rides, and savored s’mores around campfires at the beach. In 1973, Mark Hoffman succeeded his uncle, Fred Maxwell, as President of Maxwell GallerColleen Hoffman passed away on September 19, 2025. ies, which specialized in 19thand 20th-century American and European art, as well as turn-ofthe-century and contemporary California art. That same year, they moved to Piedmont, where their three daughters attended the local middle and high schools. Colleen became a docent at the Oakland Museum, developing a deep appreciation and expertise in early and modern California art. In the early 1980s, she joined her husband at Maxwell Galleries, becoming an integral part of its operations. She treated every staff member as family and built lasting client relationships. After Mark’s passing, Colleen found love again and married Bob Saydah. Their years together were filled with frequent family gatherings, meaningful friendships, world travel, bridge, and an abundance of shared laughter. They delighted in attending their grandchildren’s football and soccer games and school performances, cheering them on with pride. Colleen’s compassion, loyalty, and wholehearted dedication touched everyone she met. Her legacy lives on in the beauty she nurtured through family, friendship, art, and her unwavering belief in the goodness of life. She is survived by her daughters, Cheri Betts (Mike), Cindy Mascheroni (Tim), and Lauri Bunting; ten grandchildren; and ten great-grandchildren, all of whom brought her endless joy. She is also survived by her siblings Kathy French, Pat Dunning, and Mike Hughes. She was preceded in death by her husbands, Mark Hoffman and Bob Saydah, her parents Tom and Gertrude Pugh, and her brothers Tom Pugh and Jim Hughes. A private memorial service will be held on November 29th at St. Anselm’s Church in Lafayette, CA. Hosted by PEF’s 50th Board and co-chaired by Rich Thompson and Cameron Wolfe Jr., the event brought together generations of supporters to reflect on PEF’s legacy and the many individuals who have shaped it. Guests included current and former Board members, City and School District officials, past employees and Lifetime Donors – all united by a shared commitment to educational excellence. Thompson served as master of ceremonies, guiding the evening’s reflections and recognitions. Wolfe, one of PEF’s early Board presidents, shared stories from the organization’s founding and honored early leaders such as Helen Breck, PEF’s second president and longtime member until 1988, and Steffi Moores, the third president who launched PEF’s first major fundraising campaign in 1981. “This room is full of heroes who have carried on the work of the early volunteers,” said Wolfe. “PEF has been vital to the creation of a top-flight school district that has changed the character of the city of Piedmont.” Bridget Schreiber, current Chair of the PEF Board, expressed gratitude to the many individuals who have sustained PEF’s mission over the years. She recognized the lasting impact of volunteer leadership and announced Eileen Ruby as PEF’s newest Honorary Board Member. Ruby served on the Board from 1997–2003 and again from 2013–2023, and helped launch the PEF Endowment Fund in 1989, which today contributes roughly 10% of PEF’s annual grant to the Piedmont Unified School District. Testing is expected to resume later this week,” explained Piedmont City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. Once the heating system receives its replacement parts and resumes testing, the pool systems will start integrated testing to confirm all systems are operational. Moore described the importance of this testing. “Integrated testing involves a range of scenario-based stress tests designed to simulate sustained public use. This phase takes time but is essential to ensuring reliable long-term operations,” she said. After all testing is complete, the pool will be handed off to a Piedmont Aquatics Operations Team. They will then conduct technical systems training for more than 100 hours. This intensive technical training for city staff members will include the electrical, mechanical, and control systems that run the facility. The Operations team will conduct multi-week on-site training for lifeguards and other daily staff and will focus on daily operational procedures, including emergency response drills, lifeguard rotations, and customer service. The community pool has two pools. One for activity and one for competition. The shallower activity pool will be for kids and swim lessons for learners. The activity pool’s warmer water will be useful for recreational swimmers, looking to not freeze as they take their laps around the pool. The competition pool is 12 lanes starting at seven feet of depth to 12.5 feet at the diving well. Each lane will be 25 yards long for competitive swimming, and the pool is the regulation size for water polo matches. The pool will have an electric scoreboard for swim meets and water polo matches. So the impact on travel will be profound as we go into the holidays,” McCarthy added. Food insecurity has impacted many throughout the Bay Area. With the Federal Government’s shutdown, programs like SNAP and food banks across the Bay Area have felt the reverberating impacts. Recipients of these programs are at immediate risk of food insecurity. Fortunately, many Piedmonters have organized to help support the people most impacted by food insecurity. “We have many Piedmont residents who are organizing to find ways to supply and compensate for the lack of food resources to our neighboring communities. Some folks in town have connections to certain schools in Oakland or food banks in Oakland that they’re connected with, and they’re asking their Piedmont neighbors to be generous and help donate gift cards for grocery stores,” McCarthy noted. With the shutdown continuing, there is a strain put on the community. Food insecurity, a lack of reliable transportation, health care, and federal workers are all points of impact in the shutdown. McCarthy made clear her desire for the shutdown to end. “I think I’m in the same mindset as everyone else. It has to end sooner rather than later, but I’m hoping it doesn’t extend beyond early next week,” she said. “I think the strain on our communities is more impactful every day the longer federal workers go unpaid, and federally funded services are left in limbo, as well as projects. Kid volunteers in front: Claire Hagerty (left), Willem Scholten, Connor Tornatore, Grayson Fishman, and Aiden Rochwerger. The Wildwood Dads Club celebrated a record-breaking year in participation, sales and smiles from the 2025 Pumpkin Patch at Coaches Field. Eighty-six adult and dozens of children volunteered over 148 shifts at the patch, resulted in $67,000 in sales. Patch Papas, the dads in charge of the pumpkin patch this year, were Brian Fischer, Dave Rochwerger, and Mike Hagerty. The sales of 6,981 pumpkins brought in over $67,000 which is 24% higher than the previous record, 2024’s sales of $54,000 and 5,570 pumpkins. “We loved helping customers ‘build a pile’ of items up front, explaining the funny varietal names, and filling trunks with more than they can carry,” said Hagerty, the club Co-President. Dedicated Wildwood dads Anthony Guarino, Nat Reinke, Sergio Serna, and Matt Derrigo also put in the high energy and effort to run the patch and fill in shifts when needed. The patch remained staffed and ready for massive crowds of pumpkin hawkers descending on the patch without notice. The best single day of sales was Sunday, October 26 and brought in $8,002. All proceeds from the patch go to Wildwood Elementary School to help fund important projects. Proceeds to the school include $20,000 for an updated computer lab of laptops, software, monitors, and peripherals installed. Dads Club and Wildwood Parents Club funding also donated $19,000 for three chillable water bottle filling stations and a lower playground fountain coming soon. Another $10,000 in donations are earmarked for updates in the auditorium including updated amps, wireless mics, and a projector. $3,500 in donations are going to the inclusion room, new MPR chairs, and a new dishwasher in the staff lounge. The final profit from the patch will be calculated after final invoices arrive. While the fiscal impact is larger, so are the memories made and the smiles of kids picking out their very own Halloween pumpkins to take home.
